system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2180-01-24 03:01:00 to 2180-01-26 15:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ female status post recent laparoscopic surgery for
suspected paraduodenal hernia.  Per the surgical resident, no hernia was
noted, though there was a colonic mesenteric defect which was repaired.

COMPARISON:  ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT imaging of the abdomen and pelvis following administration of
130 cc of Optiray intravenous contrast, with preparation and review of
multiplanar reformats.

FINDINGS:

The visualized lung bases are unremarkable, without consolidation or effusion.
Heart demonstrates no pericardial effusion.

The liver is unremarkable, without focal lesions.  There is no intra- or
extra-hepatic biliary ductal dilatation.  The patient is status post
cholecystectomy.  The portal and hepatic veins are widely patent.

The spleen, pancreas, kidneys, and right adrenal gland are normal.  There is a
stable left adrenal nodule, incompletely characterized on this study.

An NG tube is seen entering the body of the stomach.  There is postsurgical
change at the gastroesophageal junction, likely reflecting prior
fundoplication.  The distal esophagus is slightly patulous.  The second and
third portions of the duodenum have a similar configuration to the prior
study, with decreased dilatation of these loops.  The second and third
portions of the duodenum do appear slightly redundant.  There is no evidence
for a paraduodenal hernia on the current study.  The intra-abdominal loops of
small bowel are unremarkable, without bowel distention or small bowel wall
thickening.

The colon has an atypical lie, with the cecum located in the left upper
quadrant.  This is not changed from prior studies, and of note, the cecum is
less distended than it has been previously, with no concern for cecal volvulus
at this time.  There is apparent diffuse colonic wall thickening involving the
transverse colon, but this is most likely reflective of underdistention.

The aorta demonstrates mild atherosclerosis but is normal in caliber.  Again
identified is a focal dissection of the superior mesenteric artery (2:33). 
This does not appear substantially changed from prior study, and the SMA
remains patent.

There is no free fluid or free air in the abdomen.  There are no loculated
fluid collections to suggest abscess formation.

There is a small umbilical fat-containing hernia.  Additional stranding and
inflammatory change are identified at the patient's prior port sites.  There
is no port site hernia identified beyond that described at the umbilicus. 
There is scattered air seen in the soft tissues, including tracking to the
left groin.  Clinical correlation is recommended, though this may represent
air tracking from recent laparoscopic surgery.  There is no associated
inflammatory change or fluid collection seen with this subcutaneous air.

CT PELVIS:  Rectum and sigmoid colon are remarkable for scattered diverticula,
and as mentioned, equivocal wall thickening.  However, the wall thickening is
more apparent at the flexures and involving the transverse colon.  The uterus
is surgically absent.  The distal ureters and bladder appear unremarkable. 
There is no pelvic fluid or pelvic adenopathy.

BONE WINDOWS:  Degenerative changes are identified in the thoracolumbar spine,
with marked loss of disc height at L4-L5.  There are no suspicious lytic or
sclerotic osseous lesions identified.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No evidence of postsurgical complication, including no free air, free
fluid, or evidence of abscess formation.  There is a small fat-containing
hernia at the umbilical port site, of doubtful significance.
2.  Apparent colonic wall thickening most likely reflects underdistention.
3.  Redemonstration of focal SMA dissection, unchanged.  The SMA appears
patent.
4.  Atypically configured bowel loops in the region of the second portion of
the duodenum, less distended than on prior study, and on the current study
clearly representing redundant duodenal loops rather than a paraduodenal
hernia.
5.  Abnormal colonic lie, with the cecum positioned in the left upper
quadrant.  There is no cecal distention, giving a low suspicion for cecal
volvulus.
6.  Status post cholecystectomy and Nissen fundoplication.
7.  Stable left adrenal nodule.

TYPE OF EXAMINATION:  Chest, AP portable, single view.

INDICATION:  ___ female patient with NG tube.  Assess placement.

FINDINGS:  The present AP single view obtained with patient in sitting
semi-upright position demonstrates the presence of an NG tube reaching far
below the diaphragm.  The tip of the line escapes the lower limit of the image
field and thus as well reached the stomach.  Chest findings in comparison with
the previous study of ___ are unaltered.  Thus, moderate elongation of
the thoracic aorta without local contour abnormalities.  No cardiac
enlargement.  No pulmonary congestion or pleural effusion.  Surgical clips
overlying left axillary area unaltered.  Surgical clips in the left upper
abdominal quadrant also unchanged.

IMPRESSION:  Well-placed NG tube.  No pneumothorax or any other
placement-related complication.

HISTORY:  Nausea and vomiting.

COMPARISON:  Radiograph ___ and CT abdomen ___.

SUPINE AND UPRIGHT ABDOMEN:
There is residual contrast noted in loops of small and large bowel.  Bowel gas
pattern is nonobstructive with air seen in non-dilated loops of small and
large bowel.  Surgical clips are noted in the left upper quadrant.  There is
no free intraperitoneal air or pneumatosis.  A nasogastric tube is seen in
appropriate position.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of bowel obstruction.  No free intraperitoneal air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you’ve been having nausea and vomiting since this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since about 8 AM. I was vomiting every 15 minutes and couldn’t keep anything down. The pain is back too—burning, right here in the upper belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you had laparoscopic surgery five days ago for a possible hernia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they thought it was a paraduodenal hernia, but said they didn’t find one. They fixed a defect in the colon instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. The CT scan from the ER shows no signs of a surgical complication—no free air, no abscess. The surgeons reviewed it and think this is likely a flare-up of your gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not from the surgery? I was worried something went wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the imaging doesn’t show any issues from the surgery. Your symptoms match what you’ve had before—chronic nausea and delayed stomach emptying. We’re going to admit you for a few days to help control it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had this for years. But it’s been worse lately, and I’ve lost weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s common with gastroparesis. We’ve placed a nasogastric tube to rest your stomach and will give you IV fluids and anti-nausea medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube is uncomfortable, but I’ll do what I need to. What medicine are you giving me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started IV Zofran, 8 mg. It’s helped many patients like you. We’ll keep monitoring and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. How are you feeling this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I haven’t vomited since the tube was placed, and the nausea is much less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. The chest X-ray confirmed the NG tube is in the right place. We also checked your labs—your potassium is a bit low, so we’re adding some to your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I’ve been feeling weak?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Low potassium can cause fatigue and muscle weakness. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The abdominal X-ray shows no obstruction. Air is moving through your bowels, and the NG tube is still in place. This supports that it’s gastroparesis, not a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. Can I try drinking something soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We want to keep your stomach at rest for now. But you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your nausea has been gone for over 24 hours. We’re going to stop the NG tube and start you on clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great! Can I have water or broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small sips at first. We’ll see how you tolerate it. If you do well, we’ll advance to a soft diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about my regular meds? I take omeprazole, Celexa, and Synthroid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been giving you those by mouth since yesterday. Your thyroid and acid reflux are stable, so we’re continuing them as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your gastroenterologist came by this morning. He agrees this is a gastroparesis flare. He recommends continuing your dromperidone and eating six small, low-fat meals a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing that, but it’s hard to stick to. Are there any other treatments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: He mentioned a repeat gastric emptying study could help guide future treatment, but for now, diet and medication are the mainstays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try. My blood pressure has been high lately too—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed your diastolic pressure was elevated, but we didn’t start new meds. Your primary doctor should check it after you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well on the soft diet. No nausea or vomiting. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What should I do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your regular medications. Stick to small, frequent, low-fat meals. Advance your diet slowly as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start feeling sick again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your gastroenterologist or primary doctor. If it’s severe, go to the ER. But you’re in much better shape now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning are stable. We’ve updated your discharge meds—omeprazole is now 20 mg instead of 40, but everything else is the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that okay? I’ve been on 40 mg for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your reflux is well-controlled, and 20 mg is sufficient. It’s a common adjustment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And I should follow up with my PCP and gastroenterologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They’ll help manage your gastroparesis long-term. We’ll send them a summary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re discharging you home today. Take it easy, eat small meals, and keep up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this wasn’t something serious from the surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT and exam confirmed no surgical complications. This was a recurrence of your chronic condition, well-managed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ll be more careful with my diet going forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do. And reach out if symptoms return—we’re here to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we hope not to see you back soon!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same here. Have a good day!

summary.summary_paragraph: A 55-year-old woman was admitted for recurrent nausea and vomiting five days after laparoscopic repair of a colonic mesenteric defect. Initial evaluation, including CT imaging, ruled out postoperative complications or bowel obstruction. Symptoms were attributed to a flare of chronic gastroparesis. She was managed with NG tube placement, IV fluids, and antiemetics, showing improvement within 24 hours. The NG tube was removed on hospital day two, and her diet was advanced successfully. Her gastroenterologist recommended continued dromperidone and a low-fat, small-meal diet. She was discharged home on day three with stable vital signs, no nausea, and a plan to follow up with her primary care provider and gastroenterologist. No medication changes were made except for reducing omeprazole from 40 mg to 20 mg daily.
